title: The first five minutes: what to establish before touching anything
content:
Every investigation that goes badly goes badly in the first five minutes, by starting on a theory instead of a fact. Five things, in this order, before reading any code.

WHAT IS THE ACTUAL SYMPTOM, stated as an observation rather than a diagnosis. Registration is broken is a diagnosis. This account submitted a code at this time and received this response is an observation. If the report only contains diagnoses, go back and get an observation, because the diagnosis is usually somebody's guess and it will steer you for an hour.

WHEN DID IT START, and what is the evidence for that boundary. Not when it was noticed. A symptom noticed today may have started at a change last week, and the gap between those two is where the cause lives. Anchor it to the last known-good observation, not to the first complaint.

WHAT CHANGED AROUND THAT TIME. Deploys, applied routines, configuration, third-party changes, and data volume. Note that here a routine can be replaced with no deploy at all, so the deploy history is only half the change history.

HOW MANY SUBJECTS. One user, one route, one category, or everything. This single question decides the whole investigation -- one subject points at data about that subject, everything points at a shared dependency -- and it is cheap to answer and constantly skipped.

WHAT IS THE CURRENT TIME IN UTC, read from the database. Every window you are about to use depends on it, the operating timezone is four hours ahead, and a window computed from a local clock has produced hours of chasing failures that were repaired before the window opened.

Only then form a theory. A theory formed before these five is a guess wearing a lab coat, and the cost is not that it is wrong -- it is that it makes every subsequent observation get read as confirmation.

when it started, anchored to the last known-good observation, not to the first complaint
what changed -- deploys, applied routines, configuration, third parties, data volume; note a routine can change with no deploy
how many subjects -- one user, one route, one category, or everything; this decides the whole investigation
the current time in UTC read from the database; the operating timezone is four hours ahead

title: The aborted-transaction probe: verifying a write without leaving one
content:
The tool that makes it possible to test production behaviour honestly. Open a transaction, perform the write, COUNT the effect, then raise an exception carrying the counts in its message. The exception rolls the transaction back, so nothing persists, and the counts still reach you because they are in the error text.

Why this matters more than a read-only check: reading proves what the code says, and the whole discipline here is that reading proves only that the code says so. A probe that actually writes exercises the constraints, the triggers, the defaults, the permissions and the order of operations -- all the things that decide behaviour and none of which are visible in a select.

THE RULE THAT MAKES IT TRUSTWORTHY: assert the fixtures FIRST. Before measuring anything, read back what you seeded and confirm it exists with the shape you expect. A probe that skips this and then finds nothing has not measured absence, it has measured a failed setup, and the two produce identical output. This is the single most common way a probe lies.

WHAT IT CANNOT DO, stated so it is not over-trusted. It cannot verify anything that happens outside the transaction -- a message actually sent, an external call actually made, a job actually scheduled. Those escape the rollback in one direction and are not undone by it. So a probe that touches a path which sends, alerts or pages will do those things for real, and the estate has already been bitten by a rehearsal that paged the founder. Establish what a path does before probing it, and run fixtures inside whatever wrapper suppresses outbound effects.

Also: it holds locks for its duration, so a probe on a hot table during a busy period is itself an incident.

Use synthetic identities following the demo convention throughout, so that if something does escape the rollback it is unmistakably not a real participant.

structured_data.pattern: open a transaction, write, count the effect, raise an exception carrying the counts so it rolls back and the numbers still come out
structured_data.why_over_a_read: reading proves the code says so; writing exercises constraints, triggers, defaults, permissions and ordering
structured_data.critical_rule: assert the fixtures FIRST by reading them back -- a probe that skips this and finds nothing has measured a failed setup, not absence, and the output is identical
structured_data.cannot_do: anything outside the transaction -- a message sent, an external call, a scheduled job; those escape the rollback and are not undone
structured_data.hazard: a probe on an alerting path will page for real; run fixtures inside a wrapper that suppresses outbound effects
structured_data.second_hazard: it holds locks for its duration, so probing a hot table during a busy period is itself an incident
structured_data.identities: synthetic, following the demo convention, so anything that escapes is unmistakably not a real participant

title: What deployed means here, and why a successful command is not it
content:
A change is deployed when its definition has been read back out of the running system and matched against the file. Not when a command returned success. Not when a check went green. Not when the code typechecks or reads correctly.

The reason this is defined so narrowly is that every weaker definition has already failed. A command can succeed against the wrong target. A check can pass because it read nothing. A pipeline can report success for a step it skipped. Each of those looks exactly like a deploy, and the only observation that distinguishes them is comparing what is actually there to what was supposed to be there.

SO THE VERIFICATION IS ALWAYS THE SAME TWO STEPS: apply, then read the definition back and compare. For routines that is reading the body out of the database. For edge functions it is confirming the deployed code matches the repository, which the estate has a check for. For a knowledge body it is counting the rows and their properties in the database rather than counting what the loader said it wrote.

AND THE COMPANION RULE FOR BEHAVIOUR, because a matching definition still is not a working system: verify by EXECUTION, in the same turn. Call the thing. Assert on the response AND on a non-zero effect. A definition that matches and has never been executed is a deployment, not a fix.

The phrase in the same turn is doing real work in that sentence. Verification deferred to later is verification that does not happen, and a change believed to be deployed is more dangerous than one known to be pending, because nobody is watching it.

When you cannot verify -- because the path needs a credential you do not have, or an external service is down -- say that plainly and say what is unverified. An honest gap is worth more than a green tick over an assumption, and this is not a stylistic preference here, it is the standing instruction.

structured_data.definition: deployed means the definition has been read back out of the running system and matched against the file
structured_data.why_narrow: a command can succeed against the wrong target, a check can pass because it read nothing, a pipeline can report success for a skipped step -- all look identical to a deploy
structured_data.two_steps: apply, then read back and compare

by_subject.routine: read the body out of the database
by_subject.edge function: confirm the deployed code matches the repository
by_subject.knowledge body: count rows and properties in the database, not what the loader reported

structured_data.companion_rule: verify by execution in the same turn -- call it, assert on the response AND a non-zero effect
structured_data.in_the_same_turn: deferred verification does not happen, and a change believed deployed is more dangerous than one known pending
structured_data.when_you_cannot: say so plainly and name what is unverified; an honest gap beats a green tick over an assumption

title: Never state what you have not measured, and how to say a bounded result honestly
content:
The standing instruction, and it applies to findings, verdicts, commit messages, answers and offhand remarks alike: state what you measured, not what it implies.

The incident that created it is worth carrying because it is so ordinary. A search of COLUMN NAMES for demo and test markers returned nothing, and that was reported as nothing marks a row as demo today. Six clearly-marked demo suppliers had existed for weeks. The convention was in the DATA -- a marker in the name and an invalid-by-construction email domain -- not in the schema. The search was correct. The claim was about everything the search did not cover.

SO THE DISCIPLINE HAS THREE PARTS.

Name the boundary out loud, as part of the result rather than as a caveat after it. The scan covered these columns, in this schema, for these patterns, and found this. That sentence is a measurement. There is no demo data is a claim about everything you did not look at.

Do not convert a narrow check into a broad verdict. This is the same defect as an instrument measuring the wrong subject, arriving from the other direction: the number is right and the sentence built on it is bigger than the number.

And if you are not sure, either measure it or say you are not sure. Both are acceptable. What is not acceptable is confident guessing, and neither is hedged guessing -- padding an unmeasured claim with softening language so it reads as knowledge is the same failure with better manners.

This does not license endless checking or silence. Measure, then speak plainly about what you measured. The goal is that every sentence in a report can be traced to an observation, not that no sentence is ever written.

structured_data.instruction: state what you measured, not what it implies
structured_data.origin: a search of COLUMN NAMES found no demo markers and was reported as no demo data existing; six marked demo suppliers existed, marked in the DATA -- a name marker and an invalid email domain -- not in the schema
three_parts: name the boundary as part of the result, not as a caveat after it
do not convert a narrow check into a broad verdict
if unsure, measure it or say you are unsure -- confident guessing and hedged guessing are the same failure
structured_data.goal: every sentence in a report traceable to an observation

title: Root cause, not symptom: find the shared function every caller routes through
content:
A report names a symptom in one place. Fixing it there is almost always the wrong-sized change, in both directions.

Too small, because the same defect usually exists in every sibling that calls the same helper. Patching the one path the report names leaves the others broken and guarantees the ticket comes back wearing a different hat.

Too large, because the instinct after finding several instances is to guard each one. A guard in every caller is a bigger diff, a bigger review, and a bigger surface for the next person to miss a caller.

THE MOVE IS THE SAME EVERY TIME: before editing, find every caller of the function you are about to touch. Then decide where the fix belongs -- and it almost always belongs in the shared function, because one guard there is a smaller change than a guard in each caller AND it covers the callers nobody has thought of yet, including the ones written next month.

Here that shared point is usually a database routine rather than an application helper, because most rules live in routines. So the caller search runs in two places: the repository, for application call sites, and the database, for routines calling routines and for triggers. A repository search alone will miss the database-side callers entirely, which is a large fraction of them in this estate.

AND THE HONEST EXCEPTION: sometimes the shared function is genuinely right and one caller is genuinely wrong. That is a real case, not a rationalisation, and the way to tell is whether the other callers WANT the behaviour you are about to change. If they do, fix the caller. If they merely tolerate it, fix the shared function.

structured_data.problem: a report names a symptom in one place, and fixing it there is the wrong-sized change in both directions
structured_data.too_small: the same defect exists in every sibling calling the same helper
structured_data.too_large: a guard in every caller is a bigger diff and a bigger surface to miss one
structured_data.the_move: find every caller BEFORE editing, then fix at the shared point -- smaller than guarding each caller, and it covers callers not yet written
structured_data.two_searches: the repository for application call sites, and the database for routines calling routines and for triggers; a repository search alone misses a large fraction here
structured_data.honest_exception: if the other callers WANT the behaviour, fix the caller; if they merely tolerate it, fix the shared function

title: Reading a guard's refusal instead of working around it
content:
When a constraint, a foreign key, a check, a trigger or a credential test refuses an operation, the overwhelmingly likely explanation is that it is right and the operation is wrong. Every guard in this estate that has refused something has, on inspection, been correct at least as often as not -- including one that stopped a structural deletion while the thing being deleted still owned live work.

So the first response to a refusal is to READ WHAT IT SAYS, in full, including the constraint's name, which usually encodes what it protects. The second is to ask what property it exists to preserve. Only after both is it reasonable to consider that the guard might be wrong.

WHAT WORKING AROUND ONE COSTS. Disabling it for the operation removes the protection for everything else running at the same time. Adding an exception makes the guard conditional on a case that will be copied by the next person. Deleting it converts a hard refusal into a silent corruption that surfaces weeks later, somewhere else, unattributable.

SOME GUARDS ARE ASKING FOR SOMETHING RATHER THAN REFUSING. A guard that wants a change reason set in the same transaction is not an obstacle -- it is the audit trail, and providing it is the intended interaction rather than a workaround. Read the requirement before assuming it is a wall.

AND THE STANDING RULE ABOVE ALL OF THIS: never weaken a check to make it pass. A check that passes while the thing it checks is broken is worse than no check, because it converts an outage into confidence. If a fix makes a check HARDER because the old pass was false, that is correct, and the right response is to say so plainly rather than to restore the comfortable number.

structured_data.prior: a refusing guard is right at least as often as not; one stopped a structural deletion while the subject still owned live work
structured_data.first_response: read the refusal in full, including the constraint name, which usually encodes what it protects
structured_data.second: ask what property it exists to preserve
costs_of_working_around: disabling removes protection for everything else running concurrently
an exception becomes a pattern the next person copies
deleting converts a hard refusal into silent corruption that surfaces later and unattributably
structured_data.asking_not_refusing: a guard requiring a change reason in the same transaction is the audit trail, and providing it is the intended interaction
structured_data.standing_rule: never weaken a check to make it pass; a check that passes while its subject is broken converts an outage into confidence
structured_data.corollary: if a fix makes a check harder because the old pass was false, say so plainly

title: What to monitor across the app and the website when you are asked to monitor everything
content:
Monitor everything is not a specification, and treating it as one produces a wall of dashboards nobody reads. The useful translation is a small number of questions the business would want answered before a human noticed, and each needs exactly one signal.

FIRST, NAME THE SURFACES, because everything is not a place. There are four: the WEBSITE, which is the public marketing site; the APP, which is the customer portal and the supplier portal, both served by the same web application; the EDGE FUNCTIONS, which are the only network path from either portal into the database; and the SCHEDULE, which is outside all three and drives everything timed. A monitor that covers the website and the app but not the edge functions and the schedule covers what a visitor can see and none of what the business actually does.

IS THE CLOCK RUNNING. Everything timed depends on one external schedule, so this is first and it is checked by the age of the most recent effect rather than by any configuration.

CAN A CUSTOMER GET IN. The sign-in path end to end through the app, exercised synthetically with a demo identity, asserting on the effect rather than on a status code. This covers account creation, because there is no separate registration path.

CAN A CUSTOMER SUBMIT AND GET AN ANSWER. The request path and the comparison path, measured by elapsed time computed from run timestamps, tracked as a distribution rather than an average, because the tail is what people experience.

IS THE WEBSITE ITSELF SERVING, AND SERVING TRUTH. A page rendering is not evidence that anything behind it works, because reads can serve from cache or a build artefact long after the data layer is unreachable. So the website check must exercise a WRITE, not a fetch.

IS ANYTHING QUEUED AND NOT MOVING. The age of the oldest unconsumed item on every queue -- messages, notifications, anything with a pending state. Age, not depth.

DID MONEY ARRIVE AND GET RECORDED. A reconciliation between the payment provider and the local record, alerting on the DIFFERENCE, because a webhook error rate cannot see the events that never came.

IS ANYTHING BEING ATTACKED. Ratios rather than counts: code requests versus verifications, refusals from the rate limiter, distinct identifiers probed per caller, uploads failing the type check.

IS ANYTHING COSTING MORE THAN IT SHOULD. Call counts per caller per hour, because a spike pre-launch is a loop rather than demand.

ARE THE GUARDS ALIVE. Every detection has a positive control that fires on a schedule; a detector with no recent proof of life is reporting nothing, however green it looks.

Nine signals across four surfaces. Each names a subject, each has an effect it asserts on, and each would be noticed by a person within a day if it were wrong. Anything beyond these earns its place by naming a failure that these nine would miss.

title: Rolling back, and when not to
content:
A rollback is the fastest way to stop a bleeding change and the slowest way to understand one. Both halves matter.

ROLL BACK IMMEDIATELY when the change is recent, the symptom started with it, and the impact is ongoing. Understanding can wait; customers cannot. Do not spend the outage diagnosing -- restore the previous state, then diagnose against the artefact rather than against production.

BUT ESTABLISH THAT IT IS ROLLBACKABLE FIRST, because in this estate that varies by subject and getting it wrong makes things worse.

An edge function is straightforward: redeploy the previous code, and a manual dispatch is the tool when the files did not change.

A routine is replaceable but NOT versioned by any pipeline -- there is no deploy history to roll back to. The previous definition exists only if somebody kept it, which means the file in the repository at the previous commit. Applying that is the rollback, and it is a forward action that happens to restore an earlier state.

A MIGRATION THAT CHANGED DATA IS OFTEN NOT REVERSIBLE AT ALL. Dropping a column loses what was in it. Rewriting values loses the originals unless they were preserved deliberately. Before treating a data change as rollbackable, establish what would be needed to restore it, and if the answer is a backup, say so out loud rather than discovering it mid-rollback.

DO NOT ROLL BACK when the change fixed something worse, when the symptom predates it, or when rolling back would itself lose data written since. That third case is the one people miss: reverting a schema change after new rows have relied on it is not a restoration, it is a second incident.

AND AFTERWARDS: a rollback is not a fix. It is a pause. The change is still needed, the defect is still there, and the thing most likely to go wrong now is that the pause gets treated as a resolution and the same change ships again unchanged.

by_subject.data migration: often not reversible -- a dropped column loses its contents, rewritten values lose the originals; if the answer is a backup, say so before starting

structured_data.afterwards: a rollback is a pause, not a fix; the risk is that the pause is treated as a resolution and the same change ships again unchanged

title: Reading a log without drowning in it
content:
Logs are the least efficient place to start and the most efficient place to finish, and inverting that order is the most common way an investigation consumes a day.

START FROM THE EFFECT, NOT THE LOG. Ask the database what the last real outcome was and when. That single timestamp bounds the window and turns an open-ended search into a bounded one. Searching logs without a window is reading.

NORMALISE BEFORE COUNTING. The same fault appears a thousand times with a thousand different identifiers in it. Replace digits and identifier-shaped tokens with a placeholder, then group. A thousand lines become five distinct messages with counts, and the shape of the problem is visible immediately. Counting raw lines measures verbosity.

COUNT WHAT IS MISSING, NOT ONLY WHAT IS PRESENT. In this estate the run record is written at the END of work, so a crash or a timeout leaves NO row. Absence is the signal for the worst failures, and no amount of searching for error text will find them. Compare what should have produced a record against what did.

READ THE FIRST OCCURRENCE, NOT THE LOUDEST. The most frequent message is usually a downstream consequence -- retries, cascading timeouts, dependent failures. The first message in the window is usually closer to the cause. Sort by time ascending and read the beginning.

AND WATCH FOR THE LOG THAT STOPPED. A component that goes quiet looks healthy in an error search, because it has no errors. Silence from something that normally logs is a stronger signal than noise from something that normally does not, and it is invisible to every query written as a search for problems.

structured_data.principle: logs are the least efficient place to start and the most efficient place to finish

title: Deciding what to do when you cannot reproduce it
content:
An unreproducible report is not a dead end and it is not a reason to close. It is a statement that your model of the conditions is incomplete, and the conditions are the thing to hunt rather than the bug.

THE AXES THAT USUALLY EXPLAIN IT, in the order they pay off here.

DATA ABOUT THE SUBJECT. The single most productive axis. Two rows for one identity, a row in an unexpected state, a suppression entry, a consumed rate limit, an address differing by case or whitespace. Code does not discriminate between users; data does. Start here whenever the report is about one user.

TIMING AND CONCURRENCY. A race reproduces only under load or under a double submit. If the report involves anything that could have been submitted twice, assume it was.

STATE ACCUMULATED FROM EARLIER STEPS. A session, a cached response, a stored token, a partially completed earlier attempt. The reporter has a history; a fresh test does not.

ENVIRONMENT ON THE OTHER SIDE. A different client, a different network, a different clock. Weak, but real.

AND THE ONE PEOPLE FORGET: THE HARNESS. You may be unable to reproduce because your test setup constructs a state reality cannot produce -- or, in the specific case that has already cost time here, because signing a session in by hand takes a shortcut the real screens do not, and the shortcut produces behaviour the product never would. When a reproduction attempt behaves strangely, suspect the harness before the product.

WHAT TO DO WHILE IT IS UNRESOLVED. Add the observation you lacked. If you could not tell which of two rows was read, log which. If you could not tell whether it was a retry, record the attempt count. An unreproducible report whose next occurrence is fully instrumented is a solved problem waiting for a recurrence, which is a much better position than a closed ticket.

structured_data.framing: unreproducible means your model of the conditions is incomplete; hunt the conditions, not the bug

a session, a cached response, a stored token, a partial earlier attempt -- the reporter has a history, a fresh test does not
a different client, network or clock; weak but real
your setup may construct a state reality cannot produce, or take a shortcut the real screens do not -- suspect the harness before the product

title: Judging severity without a customer to ask
content:
Pre-launch, there is no user complaining and no revenue moving, so the usual severity signals are all absent. That does not make everything low severity, and treating it that way is how a launch-blocking defect sits in a backlog for a month.

THE SUBSTITUTE QUESTION: what would this cost on the first day it is exercised for real. That reframes correctly because the system's whole purpose is to be correct when it opens.

HIGHEST. Anything that would lose or corrupt data that cannot be reconstructed, anything that would take money without recording it or record money that was not taken, anything reachable by an unauthenticated caller that should not be, and anything that would silently produce a wrong answer to a customer. Silently is the operative word -- a loud failure is recoverable, a quiet wrong answer is not, because nobody knows to correct it.

HIGH. A dated failure -- something that will break on a known date with nothing scheduled to prevent it. These are the easiest to defer and the least excusable to be surprised by, because the date was knowable.

MEDIUM. Something that is broken but visible: it fails loudly, someone notices, and there is a manual path. Cost is effort, not correctness.

LOW. Something that is wasteful or untidy but produces correct outcomes.

AND THE CATEGORY THAT IS ALWAYS UNDER-RATED: a broken detector. A monitor that cannot fire is not a low-severity monitoring issue, it is the severity of whatever it was watching, because that thing is now unwatched. Rate it by its subject, not by itself.

What does NOT make something low severity: that no customer has hit it, that the table is empty, that the path is not yet in use. Those are all true of every defect in a pre-launch system, so they cannot distinguish between them.

structured_data.problem: pre-launch removes the usual severity signals, and treating everything as low is how a launch-blocking defect sits for a month

money taken without a record, or recorded without being taken

a silently wrong answer to a customer -- silence is the operative word, since a loud failure is recoverable

title: Writing the finding: what a report must contain to be worth reading
content:
A finding that cannot be acted on is a cost, not a contribution. Six elements, and the discipline is that each is an observation rather than an inference.

THE SUBJECT, named precisely. Which routine, which function, which table, which account. A finding about the comparison system is not actionable; a finding about a named cache holding zero rows is.

THE OBSERVATION, with the query or the file that produced it and the time it was taken. Anyone should be able to repeat it and get the same answer, and if they cannot, that is itself information.

THE BOUNDARY. What the measurement covered and what it did not, stated as part of the finding rather than appended as a caveat. This is what stops a narrow check becoming a broad verdict.

THE CONSEQUENCE, in terms of what it costs rather than what it is. Every re-open recomputes at full cost is a consequence. The cache is empty is an observation. Both belong, and confusing them is how a serious finding gets read as trivia.

WHAT WAS DONE ABOUT IT, because this seat acts. If it was fixed, say what changed and how it was verified. If it was contained, say what is now unreachable. If it was neither, say why -- and why must be a reason, not an absence of a reason.

WHAT IS STILL UNKNOWN. The single most useful sentence in most reports, and the most frequently omitted. Naming what you did not establish is worth more than an extra paragraph on what you did, because it tells the next reader where to start.

AND ONE PROHIBITION ABOVE ALL: never report completion that is not true. A truthful account of what is unfinished is worth more than a green tick, and manufacturing a green one -- by weakening a check, by back-dating, by re-emitting an artefact to satisfy a comparison -- is the failure this estate treats most seriously.

elements.test: a named cache holding zero rows, not the comparison system

the boundary -- what it covered and did not, as part of the finding, not a caveat
the consequence, in cost terms rather than description
what was done about it -- fixed and verified, contained, or neither with a reason
what is still unknown -- the most useful and most omitted sentence
